A_target.statement:
Let $f$ be [[Definition:Square-Integrable Function|square-integrable]] with respect to a [[Definition:Probability Measure|probability measure]] $P$.
Let $X_1, \ldots, X_n$ be [[Definition:Independent Identically Distributed|i.i.d.]] with law $P$.
Then:
:$\displaystyle \frac 1 n \sum_{i \mathop = 1}^n \map f {X_i} \to \int f \rd P$
[[Definition:Almost Surely|almost surely]], with root-mean-square error $\dfrac {\sigma_f} {\sqrt n}$.

B_source.statement:
Let $Y_1, \ldots, Y_n$ be [[Definition:Independent Identically Distributed|i.i.d.]] with finite mean.
Then the [[Definition:Sample Mean|sample mean]] $\displaystyle \bar Y_n = \frac 1 n \sum_{i \mathop = 1}^n Y_i$ estimates $\expect Y$.

substitutions.the finitely many samples: independent draws from the density being integrated against
substitutions.the empirical average: the Monte Carlo estimate of the integral

derived.unbiasedness of the empirical average: the estimate has the integral as its expectation
derived.the standard error of the average: error decaying as one over the square root of the sample count

object_map.reformulation: Replace the integral by an average over finitely many random samples, so a continuous quantity becomes a finite mean.

validity_conditions: The integral is by definition the expectation of the function under the density, so estimating the integral is estimating a mean.
The estimate is unbiased for any sample size, and consistency follows from the law of large numbers provided the function is integrable.
The one over root n rate requires finite variance and is independent of the dimension, which is the property that makes the method preferable to grid quadrature in high dimensions.
proof_plan:
Express the integral as an expectation:
:$\displaystyle \int f \rd P = \expect {\map f X}$
where $X \sim P$.

Draw i.i.d. samples $X_i \sim P$ and form:
:$\displaystyle \hat I_n = \frac 1 n \sum_{i \mathop = 1}^n \map f {X_i}$

By linearity, $\expect {\hat I_n} = \displaystyle \int f \rd P$, so $\hat I_n$ is [[Definition:Unbiased Estimator|unbiased]].
By the [[Strong Law of Large Numbers]], $\hat I_n \to \displaystyle \int f \rd P$ almost surely.

By [[Variance of Sum of Independent Random Variables|independence]]:
:$\var {\hat I_n} = \dfrac {\sigma_f^2} n$
where $\sigma_f^2 = \var {\map f X}$.
Hence the error is of order $n^{-1 / 2}$.
{{qed}}
